<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Currently, the FDA has cleared, classified, or approved no MCED tests, and research is ongoing to understand the benefits of using MCED tests in routine clinical practice. MCED tests aim to detect many types of cancer early using noninvasive methods like blood tests, which could lead to earlier treatment. However, early detection does not always improve the chance of a cure or extend life for some cancers.\20\ Follow-up tests are needed to confirm a diagnosis, and research has shown that more than half the time, no cancer could be found in people who had a positive MCED test.\21\ Clinical trial data will be critical to determine whether detection with MCED tests improves outcomes such as cancer-related survival.\22\\23\\24\ This is why retaining the Secretary's authority to require data collection and reporting, follow the evidence, and adjust coverage accordingly is critical in this bill.

\24\Cancer Screening Overview--NCI.
The National Cancer Institute (NCI) launched the Cancer Screening Research Network (CSRN) to evaluate emerging cancer screening technologies. The CSRN will conduct multi-center cancer screening trials with diverse populations in various health care settings to reduce cancer-related illnesses and deaths.\25\ In 2025, the CSRN launched the Vanguard study, a pilot study to assess the feasibility of using MCED tests in future randomized controlled trials. This study will enroll up to 24,000 people to inform the design of a larger trial, which will evaluate whether the benefits of using MCED tests outweigh the harms and whether the tests can reduce cancer deaths.\26\ Medicare also has the authority to cover the costs of such tests in clinical trials.
